entry.title: New Puppy Care: Your First 30 Days | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: A calm, practical first-month puppy checklist covering settling in, feeding, sleep, toilet routines, socialization and veterinary care.
entry.content:
← Pawwise Daily home

PUPPY CARE · 8 MIN READ

Your puppy’s first 30 days: a gentle, practical plan

A new puppy needs safety, patience and predictable routines more than a perfect schedule. Use this guide as a flexible starting point, and adapt it to your puppy’s age, health and personality.

Updated November 19, 2026 · Pawwise Daily Editorial Team. This educational guide is not individually veterinary reviewed and does not replace advice from your veterinarian.

Before your puppy arrives

Prepare a quiet sleeping area, food and water bowls, a suitable puppy food, a comfortable harness or collar, an identification tag, safe chew toys and cleaning supplies. Puppy-proof the home: secure electrical cords, medicines, cleaning products, small objects and anything your puppy might chew or swallow. Choose a veterinarian and save the clinic’s contact details.

Days 1–3: keep life calm

Give your puppy time to explore one safe area at a time. Keep visitors and exciting outings to a minimum. Offer the same food the puppy has been eating, unless a veterinarian advises otherwise. Let the puppy rest often; young puppies need substantial sleep. Take them to the toilet after waking, eating, drinking and playing, and praise them calmly when they go in the right place.

Remember: Accidents are normal while a puppy learns. Clean the area thoroughly and return to a predictable toilet routine. Never punish or frighten a puppy for an accident.

Week 1: build predictable routines

Use regular times for meals, toilet breaks, gentle play and rest. Keep training sessions very short. Reward the puppy for responding to its name, coming toward you and calmly settling. Introduce a crate or pen gradually as a comfortable resting space; never use it as punishment and make sure the puppy has appropriate toilet breaks.

Weeks 2–3: introduce the world safely

Positive early experiences can help puppies grow into confident adults. Let your puppy hear ordinary household sounds at a comfortable distance, meet calm people, and explore different safe surfaces. Pair new experiences with treats and the option to move away. Ask your veterinarian which places and interactions are appropriate before your puppy has completed its vaccination course. Avoid dog parks and areas with unknown vaccination status until your veterinarian says they are safe.

Week 4: strengthen good habits

Continue reward-based training, gentle handling of paws and ears, and calm grooming introductions. Practice brief periods of settling alone while staying within your puppy’s comfort level. Increase walks and activity only in line with veterinary advice and your puppy’s development; avoid forced or strenuous exercise.

Food, water and health

Choose a complete puppy food appropriate for growth and follow feeding guidance as a starting point. Fresh water should always be available. Arrange a veterinary visit soon after bringing your puppy home to discuss examination, vaccinations, parasite prevention, microchipping, dental care and a suitable follow-up schedule. Do not give human medicines or supplements unless your veterinarian specifically recommends them.

When to contact a veterinarian

Contact a veterinarian promptly if your puppy is repeatedly vomiting, has persistent diarrhea, refuses food, seems unusually weak, or has a sudden change in behaviour. Difficulty breathing, collapse, seizures, severe bleeding or suspected poisoning are emergencies—seek urgent veterinary help.

A simple daily puppy checklist

  • Feed measured, age-appropriate meals and provide fresh water.
  • Offer frequent toilet opportunities and reward success.
  • Provide gentle play, sniffing and short positive training.
  • Allow plenty of uninterrupted rest.
  • Check appetite, energy, stool and behaviour.
  • Keep the environment safe and comfortable.

This article is general educational information, not a substitute for veterinary advice. Your veterinarian can tailor a plan to your puppy.

entry.title: How to Set Up a Cat Litter Box | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: A practical guide to choosing, placing and cleaning a cat litter box, with signs that a litter-box problem may need veterinary attention.
entry.content:
← Pawwise Daily home

CAT CARE · 6 MIN READ

How to set up a cat-friendly litter box

A clean, accessible litter box in a calm location can make everyday life easier for both cats and people. Small details—such as box size, litter texture and placement—can matter.

Updated November 19, 2026 · Pawwise Daily Editorial Team. This educational guide is not individually veterinary reviewed and does not replace advice from your veterinarian.

1. Start with enough boxes

A commonly recommended starting point is one litter box per cat, plus one extra. In a multi-cat home, place boxes in more than one location rather than lining them all up together. This gives cats options and can reduce competition.

2. Choose a box your cat can use comfortably

Many cats prefer a roomy, simple, uncovered box. A large cat may need a larger tray, while a kitten, senior cat or cat with mobility difficulty may need a low entry. If you are unsure what your cat prefers, offer a suitable alternative and observe which one is used.

3. Consider unscented litter

Many cats prefer unscented, finer-textured litter. If you are changing litter, do it gradually rather than making a sudden switch. Avoid strong fragrances intended to mask odors; a clean box and good placement are usually a better starting point.

4. Pick a quiet, accessible location

Choose a calm spot that your cat can reach at all times. Keep litter boxes away from food and water bowls, noisy appliances and places where another pet could block the exit. Older cats or cats with mobility problems may need a box on each floor they use.

5. Keep the box clean

Remove waste at least daily and refresh the litter as needed. Wash the tray periodically with a gentle, unscented cleaner, rinse it well and dry it before refilling. Replace trays that are cracked or retain odors that cannot be removed.

6. If your cat stops using the box, look for a cause

Do not assume it is misbehavior. The box may be dirty, difficult to reach, in an uncomfortable location, or filled with litter your cat dislikes. Conflict with another pet can also make a box feel unsafe. A sudden change in toileting can also be related to pain or illness.

Important health warning: Straining to urinate, repeated trips to the box with little or no urine, crying while trying to urinate, or an inability to pass urine can signal an emergency—especially in male cats. Seek urgent veterinary care. Any new or persistent litter-box change deserves a call to your veterinarian.

A quick litter-box checklist

  • Enough boxes, placed in separate quiet locations.
  • A roomy box with an entry your cat can manage.
  • Unscented litter if your cat prefers it.
  • Waste removed daily and trays kept clean.
  • Food and water kept separate from litter areas.
  • Sudden toileting changes discussed with a veterinarian.

Further reading

For more detail, see the Cornell Feline Health Center guide to house-soiling and its information on feline lower urinary tract disease.

This article is general educational information, not a diagnosis or treatment plan. Consult a licensed veterinarian about your individual cat.

entry.title: How to Brush Your Dog’s Teeth: A Gentle Step-by-Step Guide | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Learn how to introduce tooth brushing to your dog gradually, choose pet-safe supplies, build a routine and recognize signs that need a veterinary dental check.
entry.content:
← Pawwise Daily home

DOG HEALTH · 7 MIN READ

How to brush your dog’s teeth: a gentle step-by-step guide

Tooth brushing can feel unfamiliar to a dog at first. The goal is not to finish a perfect brushing session on day one. Build comfort in small steps, use supplies made for pets, and ask your veterinarian to check your dog’s mouth regularly.

Updated November 19, 2026 · Pawwise Daily Editorial Team. This educational guide is not individually veterinary reviewed and does not replace advice from your veterinarian.

Why dental care matters

Plaque collects on teeth and can harden into tartar. Dental disease may cause discomfort, gum inflammation, loose or damaged teeth, and difficulty eating. Dogs do not always show obvious signs of mouth pain, so routine veterinary dental checks are important even when your dog seems happy.

The American Veterinary Medical Association recommends that a veterinarian check your pet’s teeth and gums at least once a year. Your dog may need an earlier examination if you notice persistent bad breath, red or bleeding gums, loose or broken teeth, unusual drooling, dropping food, or reluctance to eat.

What you need

  • A soft-bristled pet toothbrush or a small, soft toothbrush that fits your dog comfortably.
  • Toothpaste specifically formulated for dogs.
  • Small rewards and a calm, unhurried place.
Important: Do not use human toothpaste. Dogs swallow what is put in their mouths, and human toothpaste is not designed for them. Never use baking soda or household dental products as a substitute for pet toothpaste.

Introduce brushing in small steps

Step 1: Make mouth handling feel normal

Choose a quiet moment when your dog is relaxed. Briefly touch the side of the muzzle, praise your dog, and offer a reward. Repeat for a few seconds at a time. Stop while your dog is still comfortable. If your dog pulls away, growls, snaps, or seems worried, do not force the interaction.

Step 2: Gently lift the lip

When muzzle touches are easy, briefly lift the lip to look at the teeth. Reward calm behaviour and keep sessions short. You do not need to open your dog’s mouth wide to begin.

Step 3: Introduce the pet toothpaste

Let your dog sniff the toothbrush and taste a tiny amount of dog toothpaste from your finger or the brush, following the product directions. Pair this with praise. The aim is to make the new taste and tool familiar.

Step 4: Brush a few teeth

Start with just a few outer tooth surfaces, especially the teeth along the cheek side. Use gentle, small movements and a soft brush. Gradually add more teeth over several sessions as your dog accepts the routine. Never wrestle the mouth open or continue if your dog appears painful or distressed.

Step 5: Build a repeatable routine

Daily brushing is the ideal goal. If that is not realistic at first, establish a calm routine and ask your veterinarian what level of home care is appropriate for your dog. Consistency matters more than attempting a long session that your dog fears.

What if your dog will not accept a toothbrush?

Go back to an easier step and progress more slowly. Some dogs need more time or a different brush shape. If handling the mouth is unsafe, stop and ask your veterinary team for help. Your veterinarian may discuss other options, such as products carrying the Veterinary Oral Health Council (VOHC) seal, dental diets, or dental chews suited to your dog. These options should be selected with professional advice and do not replace a veterinary examination.

When to book a dental check

Arrange a veterinary appointment if you notice ongoing bad breath, red or swollen gums, visible tartar, mouth bleeding, pawing at the face, unusual drooling, chewing on one side, dropping food, or a change in appetite. A dog with a painful mouth may resist handling, so do not try to scrape tartar off at home.

Professional care: A proper veterinary dental assessment may require examination and cleaning below the gumline, sometimes with dental X-rays and anesthesia. “Anesthesia-free” scraping cannot provide the same assessment or treatment. Ask your veterinarian to explain the recommended plan and its risks and benefits for your dog.

A simple weekly habit tracker

  • Choose a regular, calm time for dental care.
  • Use only a dog-safe toothbrush and dog toothpaste.
  • Reward cooperation and keep each session positive.
  • Record any new mouth or eating changes.
  • Keep up with veterinary dental checks.

Trusted further reading

  • American Veterinary Medical Association: Pet Dental Care
  • American Animal Hospital Association: Your Pet’s Dental Care
  • Veterinary Oral Health Council: Accepted dental products

This article is general educational information, not a diagnosis or treatment plan. Your veterinarian can tailor dental care to your individual dog.

entry.title: 10 Easy Indoor Enrichment Games for Dogs | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Keep your dog curious indoors with 10 simple enrichment games using everyday items, plus safety tips for puppies, seniors and enthusiastic chewers.
entry.content:
← Pawwise Daily home

DOG ENRICHMENT · 8 MIN READ

10 easy indoor enrichment games to keep your dog busy

Rainy day, small apartment, or a quiet afternoon at home? A few minutes of sniffing, searching and learning can make indoor time more interesting for many dogs. You do not need expensive equipment: start with safe household items and a little of your dog’s usual food.

Updated November 19, 2026 · Pawwise Daily Editorial Team. This educational guide is not individually veterinary reviewed and does not replace advice from your veterinarian.

Start with your dog, not the game. Choose activities that match your dog’s age, confidence, mobility and chewing habits. Keep sessions short and enjoyable. Enrichment should offer choice and curiosity—not frustration or pressure.

Before you begin: four simple safety rules

  • Supervise closely. Watch your dog with boxes, towels, toys and food puzzles. Remove anything that is being shredded or swallowed.
  • Use dog-safe food. The easiest reward is part of your dog’s normal daily food allowance. Introduce unfamiliar foods cautiously and check with your veterinarian if your dog has allergies, a medical condition or a prescribed diet.
  • Keep it easy at first. Let your dog succeed quickly. If they become frustrated, make the task simpler or take a break.
  • Make space safe. Use a non-slip surface, keep small objects and electrical cords away, and avoid games that encourage jumping or hard twisting—especially for puppies, seniors or dogs with mobility problems.

10 low-cost games to try at home

GAME 01 · SNIFFING2–5 minutes

1. The treat treasure hunt

Ask your dog to wait in another room or have someone gently hold their harness. Place a few pieces of their usual kibble in easy-to-find spots around one safe room. Release your dog with a cheerful cue such as “Find it.” Start with visible pieces, then make the hiding places slightly less obvious as your dog understands the game.

Make it easier: Put the food on the floor in plain sight. Make it harder: Hide pieces beside furniture legs or behind a safe, stable object—not inside places your dog could get stuck.

GAME 02 · FORAGING3–5 minutes

2. The towel roll

Lay a clean towel flat, scatter a small handful of kibble across it, then loosely fold or roll the towel so food is easy to uncover. Let your dog sniff and nudge it open while you supervise. Use a towel only if your dog does not chew or eat fabric.

Safety note: Skip this game for dogs that swallow cloth, pull threads or become possessive around food. Never leave a fabric puzzle unattended.

GAME 03 · PROBLEM-SOLVING2–4 minutes

3. The open-box search

Put a few kibble pieces in a clean, empty cardboard box with all staples, tape and labels removed. Leave the top fully open and let your dog investigate. For a beginner, use a large box with no flaps to push through.

Safety note: Supervise every moment and remove the box if your dog eats cardboard. Do not use boxes with plastic film, sharp edges, staples or packing materials.

GAME 04 · CHOICE2–3 minutes

4. Which hand?

Place one piece of kibble in one closed hand. Offer both closed hands at your dog’s nose level and wait for a gentle sniff or touch. Open the correct hand and reward. Switch hands between turns. Keep your hands relaxed and never tease or make your dog paw forcefully.

GAME 05 · TRAINING1–3 minutes

5. Teach a simple new cue

Choose one easy behaviour, such as touching your open palm with their nose. Present your hand a few inches away; when your dog investigates or touches it, say “Yes” and reward. Repeat a few times, then stop while your dog is still interested. A new cue is a tiny learning project, not an obedience test.

GAME 06 · SCENT WORK2–5 minutes

6. The cup find

Place one piece of kibble under one of two sturdy, lightweight, non-breakable cups while your dog watches. Invite them to find it. Keep the cups upright and allow your dog to nudge rather than paw hard. If your dog mouths or breaks the cups, stop and choose another game.

GAME 07 · CALM PLAY2–5 minutes

7. Find your toy

Show your dog a familiar toy, place it a short distance away in plain sight, and say “Find your toy.” Praise them when they reach it. Gradually place it partly behind a safe object. Do not hide toys where your dog must climb, jump or squeeze into tight spaces.

GAME 08 · BODY AWARENESS1–2 minutes

8. Follow the slow hand

Hold a treat near your dog’s nose and slowly move your hand a short distance left or right, inviting them to follow with their nose. Reward a gentle turn. Keep movements small and comfortable; do not spin your dog in circles or ask for movements that cause discomfort.

GAME 09 · SETTLING1–3 minutes

9. Relax on a mat

Put a comfortable mat on a quiet, non-slip floor. When your dog steps onto it or chooses to lie down, calmly place a piece of kibble between their paws. Reward relaxed moments without repeatedly asking for a position. Let your dog leave whenever they want.

GAME 10 · SOCIAL CONNECTION2–4 minutes

10. The name-and-reward game

Say your dog’s name once in a friendly voice when they are not distracted. When they look toward you, say “Yes” and reward. Try a few repetitions in different quiet rooms. If they do not respond, move closer or reduce distractions instead of repeating the name louder.

How to build a simple indoor routine

You do not need to do all ten games in one day. Try one sniffing game and one short training or settling activity, then give your dog time to rest. Rotate activities across the week so they stay fresh. On days when your dog is unwell, recovering from surgery or showing pain, ask your veterinarian what activity is appropriate.

Example 10-minute session:
2 minutes of treat treasure hunt → 3 minutes of towel or box search (only if safe for your dog) → 2 minutes practicing a familiar cue → 3 minutes of calm rest. Stop sooner if your dog loses interest or seems tired.

How do you know if a game is a good fit?

Look for relaxed body language, voluntary participation and an easy return to rest. If your dog freezes, repeatedly walks away, pants heavily when not hot, shows escalating frustration, guards the food, or tries to swallow game materials, calmly end the activity and choose something simpler. Sudden behaviour changes or signs of pain deserve veterinary advice.

What indoor games should you avoid?

  • Games with small objects that could be swallowed or become choking hazards.
  • Unsupervised fabric, cardboard or plastic puzzles for dogs that chew and ingest materials.
  • Repeated high jumps, slippery-floor chasing or rough wrestling in a cramped room.
  • Food challenges that make your dog panic, guard resources or become frustrated.
  • Using human foods, supplements or treats that are unsafe for dogs.

Frequently asked questions

Can indoor games replace walks?

Usually not. Enrichment can complement appropriate exercise, toilet breaks and outdoor experiences, but it does not automatically replace them. Follow your veterinarian’s advice about activity for your dog’s age and health.

How often should I play enrichment games?

There is no single schedule for every dog. Several short, positive opportunities can work better than one long session. Watch your dog’s interest and energy, and make sure games do not replace sleep and quiet time.

What if my dog does not understand a puzzle?

Make it easier. Show the food, remove extra steps and reward any safe investigation. If your dog is not interested, try a different activity. The goal is enjoyable engagement, not solving a difficult puzzle.

Trusted further reading

  • The Humane Society of the United States: pet care tips
  • Purdue University Center for Animal Welfare Science: canine behavior resources

entry.title: West Highland White Terrier Care: Grooming, Skin & Daily Routine | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: A practical Westie care guide covering the white double coat, brushing, grooming, sensitive skin, exercise, training, dental care and health checks.
entry.content:
← Pawwise Daily home

BREED-SPECIFIC DOG CARE · 9 MIN READ

West Highland White Terrier care: a practical guide to grooming, skin and daily life

Westies are small, sturdy terriers with big personalities. Their bright white double coat, curious nature and independent streak are part of their charm—but they also mean that thoughtful grooming, consistent training and regular health checks matter. This guide explains the everyday basics without treating every dog as if it has the same needs.

Updated November 19, 2026 · Pawwise Daily Editorial Team. This educational article has not been individually veterinary reviewed and is not a substitute for advice from your veterinarian.

In this guide
  • Understand the Westie coat
  • Brushing and professional grooming
  • Look after sensitive skin
  • Exercise and enrichment
  • Training a clever terrier
  • Health checks and warning signs
  • A simple daily routine
  • Frequently asked questions

1. Understand the Westie coat

The West Highland White Terrier has a distinctive double coat: a relatively harsh outer coat over a softer undercoat. That coat is not simply decorative; it has specific maintenance needs. A pet trim and a traditional hand-stripped coat are different grooming approaches. If you prefer the traditional texture or show presentation, ask an experienced Westie groomer about hand-stripping. Many family pets are clipped for easier maintenance.

2. Brush regularly and plan professional grooming

Brush and comb your Westie several times a week, paying attention to the legs, belly, beard, behind the ears and other places where tangles can form. Work gently from the ends of a tangle rather than pulling hard against the skin. Check the coat for burrs, dirt, mats and small skin changes after walks.

Many pet Westies are professionally groomed roughly every four to six weeks, although the right interval depends on coat length, style and how quickly the coat grows. Ask the groomer to show you a simple between-visit routine. Keep nails at a comfortable length and check the ears, paws and teeth as part of normal handling.

Bathing tip: Avoid bathing on an arbitrary daily or weekly schedule. Bathe when needed with a dog-appropriate product, rinse thoroughly and dry the coat well. If your dog has itchy, inflamed or recurring skin problems, ask your veterinarian which shampoo is suitable before experimenting with products.

3. Take skin irritation seriously

Westies can be prone to allergic skin disease. Repeated scratching, paw licking, face rubbing, redness, recurring ear trouble, scabs or hair loss deserve attention. These signs do not prove that food is the cause: environmental allergens, parasites, infections and other conditions can look similar.

Keep a simple note of when symptoms happen, which areas are affected and any recent changes in food, treats, grooming products or environment. Share that history with your veterinarian. Do not start a restrictive diet, use human medication or repeatedly switch shampoos without professional guidance. A veterinarian can work out whether testing, parasite control, treatment or a properly planned diet trial is appropriate.

4. Give your Westie daily movement and sniffing time

Westies were developed as working terriers and often enjoy exploring, chasing toys and using their noses. Offer regular walks, sniffing opportunities, short play sessions and age-appropriate games. The right amount depends on your individual dog's age, fitness, health and weather conditions; build activity gradually and allow rest.

Because terriers may chase small animals or moving objects, use a leash outside unfenced areas and choose a secure enclosed space for off-leash play. In warm weather, avoid the hottest part of the day, provide water and stop if your dog seems overheated or unusually tired.

5. Make training short, upbeat and consistent

A Westie's intelligence can come with a strong independent streak. Use reward-based training, small treats from the daily food allowance, and sessions that finish before your dog loses interest. Useful skills include coming when called, walking comfortably on a leash, settling on a mat, waiting at doors and leaving unsafe objects alone.

Do not rely on punishment or repeated shouting. If barking, digging or chasing becomes difficult to manage, provide appropriate outlets and seek help from a qualified reward-based trainer. Make sure everyone in the household uses the same cues and rules.

6. Keep up with veterinary and dental care

Arrange routine veterinary examinations and ask about vaccinations, parasite prevention, dental care, weight and any breed-relevant screening. Breed organizations and veterinary references note that Westies may be affected by several conditions, including skin disease and some inherited eye, joint or other disorders. This does not mean your dog will develop them; it means regular preventive care and early discussion of changes are worthwhile.

Brush your dog's teeth with toothpaste made for dogs, ideally as part of a regular routine. Never use human toothpaste. Contact your veterinarian about persistent bad breath, gum redness, broken teeth, chewing changes, eye redness or squinting, recurring ear odor, limping, persistent coughing or changes in breathing.

Seek urgent veterinary help for difficulty breathing, collapse, seizures, severe bleeding, repeated unproductive retching or suspected poisoning. If your Westie suddenly cannot walk normally or appears to be in severe pain, contact a veterinary clinic promptly.

7. A realistic daily Westie routine

  • Morning: Fresh water, measured meal if scheduled, toilet break and a walk with time to sniff.
  • During the day: Rest, a short reward-based training session or a safe food puzzle, plus a toilet break appropriate to age and needs.
  • Evening: Another walk or play session, a quick coat and paw check, and calm time with the family.
  • Several times a week: Thorough brushing and combing; check ears, nails, skin and teeth as tolerated.
  • Regularly: Groomer appointments and preventive veterinary care tailored to your dog.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I brush a Westie?

Several times a week is a useful starting point. Dogs with longer coats or tangling may need more frequent brushing. Keep sessions gentle and positive.

How often does a Westie need professional grooming?

Many pet Westies visit a groomer about every four to six weeks. The best schedule depends on the coat style, growth and your ability to maintain the coat between visits.

Are Westies prone to skin allergies?

They can be, but itching has many possible causes. Persistent or recurring symptoms should be assessed by a veterinarian rather than treated through repeated product or diet changes at home.

Are Westies good apartment dogs?

They can adapt to different homes when their needs are met. Daily walks, sniffing, play, training and appropriate outlets for terrier instincts matter more than having a large house.

  • VCA Animal Hospitals: West Highland White Terrier

entry.title: How Often Should You Bathe a Dog? A Safe Step-by-Step Guide | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Learn how often to bathe your dog, what affects the schedule, which shampoo to use, and how to make bath time safer and calmer.
entry.content:
← Pawwise Daily home

DOG GROOMING · PRACTICAL GUIDE

How often should you bathe a dog? A safe, simple guide

🛁🐕
Quick answer: there is no one schedule for every dog.Coat type, skin health, lifestyle and how dirty your dog gets all matter.

A bath can freshen up a muddy dog, but washing too often—or using the wrong shampoo—can irritate the skin. The best routine keeps your dog comfortable without turning bath time into a weekly battle.

Updated November 19, 2026 · Pawwise Daily Editorial Team. This educational guide has not been individually veterinary reviewed and is not a substitute for advice from your veterinarian.

In this guide
  • How often is often enough?
  • What changes the schedule?
  • How to bathe a dog safely
  • Common bath-time mistakes
  • Frequently asked questions

1. How often should you bathe your dog?

Most healthy dogs need an occasional bath rather than frequent washing. A practical starting point is to bathe when your dog is visibly dirty or has developed an unpleasant odor, then adjust the routine to their coat and lifestyle. Some dogs with continuously growing or high-maintenance coats may be bathed as part of regular professional grooming; dogs with dense double coats may need more brushing and seasonal coat care than extra baths.

Veterinary guidance varies because dogs are different. VCA Animal Hospitals notes that many non-shedding breeds without skin problems are bathed around every six to eight weeks, while the ASPCA gives a general recommendation of about once every three months for many dogs. Neither interval is a rule for every dog. Follow your veterinarian or groomer's advice when your dog's breed, coat or skin needs call for a different plan.

Simple rule: If your dog is clean and comfortable, you usually do not need to bathe them just because a calendar says it is bath day. Wipe muddy paws or a small dirty patch when a full bath is unnecessary.

2. What affects your dog's bathing schedule?

  • Coat type: Long, curly or continuously growing coats often need frequent brushing and regular professional grooming. Short coats may need less coat maintenance. Double-coated dogs often benefit from thorough brushing, especially during shedding seasons.
  • Daily activities: Dogs that swim, play in mud or spend lots of time outdoors may need baths more often than dogs that mostly relax indoors.
  • Skin health: Itching, redness, flaky skin, recurring odor or ear problems should not be treated by simply bathing more. A veterinarian can check for the cause and may prescribe a specific bathing routine.
  • Age and comfort: Puppies, senior dogs and dogs with mobility concerns may need extra support, shorter sessions and a non-slip surface.

3. How to bathe a dog safely: step by step

Before the bath

Gather a dog-formulated shampoo, several towels, a cup or gentle shower attachment, and a non-slip mat. Brush the coat first to loosen dirt and small tangles. If your dog has tight mats, do not try to cut them out with scissors; ask a professional groomer or veterinarian for help.

During the bath

  1. Use comfortably lukewarm water and speak calmly. Let your dog get used to the sound and feel before wetting the whole coat.
  2. Wet the body gradually, avoiding a direct spray into the eyes, nose and ears.
  3. Apply a small amount of shampoo made specifically for dogs. Follow the product directions and avoid the eye area.
  4. Massage gently, then rinse thoroughly. Leftover shampoo can irritate the skin.
  5. Use a damp cloth to clean the face carefully rather than pouring water over it.

After the bath

Towel-dry gently and keep your dog warm until fully dry. If using a dryer, choose a low, comfortable setting, keep it moving and stop if your dog becomes distressed. Reward calm behaviour and keep the first few sessions short.

4. Common bath-time mistakes to avoid

  • Using human or baby shampoo: Choose shampoo formulated for dogs. Human products may be too harsh for canine skin.
  • Bathing repeatedly to fix itching: Persistent itching, redness or odor can have medical causes. Repeated washing may not solve the problem; ask a veterinarian.
  • Leaving shampoo behind: Rinse carefully, especially around the belly, legs and underside.
  • Forcing a frightened dog: Use gradual, reward-based introductions. If your dog panics or may bite, pause and ask a qualified groomer or veterinarian for a safer plan.
  • Ignoring mats: Mats can tighten when wet. Brush out minor tangles gently before bathing; get professional help for tight or extensive mats.

5. Frequently asked questions

Can I bathe my dog every week?

Some dogs may need a veterinarian-directed weekly bath, especially with a prescribed shampoo. For many healthy dogs, weekly shampooing is unnecessary. Ask your veterinarian if you feel your dog needs frequent baths.

Can I use my own shampoo on my dog?

No. Use a shampoo made for dogs. If your dog has sensitive skin or a diagnosed skin condition, ask your veterinarian which product is appropriate.

Should I bathe my dog after swimming?

Rinsing with clean water can help remove pool chemicals, salt or dirt from the coat. Whether a full shampoo bath is needed depends on what your dog swam in and their skin and coat. Dry your dog comfortably afterward.

What if my dog smells bad soon after a bath?

A persistent or unusual smell can come from skin, ears, mouth or another health issue. Do not keep bathing to cover it up; arrange a veterinary check.

entry.title: How to Keep Dogs and Cats Safe in Hot Weather | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: A practical, year-round guide to hot-weather safety for dogs and cats: water, shade, safer walks, hot pavement, heatstroke warning signs and when to call a vet.
entry.content:
🐾 Pawwise Daily

Dog & cat wellbeing · All climates

How to Keep Dogs and Cats Safe in Hot Weather

Hot weather does not arrive at the same time everywhere. Whether you are facing a summer heatwave, a humid tropical afternoon, or an unusually warm day, a few simple habits can help protect the animals who share your home.

Quick answer: Keep fresh water available, provide a cool and shaded place to rest, avoid strenuous activity during the hottest part of the day, check walking surfaces, and never leave an animal in a parked vehicle. If you suspect heatstroke, contact a veterinarian or emergency veterinary clinic immediately.
Found this useful?
Help another pet parent find it: Facebook · WhatsApp · LinkedIn
In this guide
  • Why heat and humidity matter
  • A simple hot-weather routine
  • Pets that need extra care
  • Warning signs of heat illness
  • What to do if you are worried

Why heat and humidity matter

Dogs and cats can struggle when their surroundings become too hot. Dogs mainly cool themselves by panting, while cats may groom and seek cooler places. High humidity can make it harder for an animal to lose heat. Heat illness can develop outdoors or inside a poorly ventilated room, vehicle, shed, or conservatory.

There is no single safe temperature for every pet. Age, body condition, coat, breed, health, activity, shade, airflow, and humidity all matter. Pay attention to the conditions where you live rather than relying on a calendar season or one temperature number.

A simple hot-weather routine

1. Make water easy to reach

Put clean, fresh water in stable bowls in places your pet can access. Check and refresh it regularly, especially outdoors where bowls can heat up, collect debris, or be knocked over. Take water and a portable bowl on outings with your dog.

2. Provide a genuinely cool place to rest

Make sure pets can move to shade and a cooler, well-ventilated indoor area. Follow the shade as it moves through the day: a spot that is shaded in the morning may be in direct sun later. Fans or air conditioning can help make an indoor space more comfortable, but never confine an animal in a hot room without a way to move to a cooler area.

3. Change the timing and intensity of exercise

Choose the coolest part of the day for walks and play, reduce the length and intensity when it is hot or humid, and take breaks. On very hot days, skip strenuous exercise and use calm indoor enrichment instead. Let your pet set the pace; do not encourage them to keep going when they slow down or seek shade.

4. Check the ground before walking

Sun-heated pavement, asphalt, sand, and other surfaces can burn paw pads. Choose shaded routes or grass where practical, and avoid surfaces that feel uncomfortably hot to your hand. Remember that a dog may be closer to the hot ground than you are.

5. Never leave a pet in a parked vehicle

A parked vehicle can become dangerously hot very quickly, even if a window is partly open or the vehicle is parked in shade. Do not leave a pet alone in a parked car while you run an errand. Plan trips so your animal can stay safely at home when they cannot accompany you.

Pets that need extra care

Any dog or cat can develop heat-related illness. Be especially cautious with flat-faced breeds, including pugs, bulldogs, and Persian cats; very young or older animals; overweight pets; animals with heart or breathing problems; and pets with thick coats or other health conditions. Ask your veterinarian for advice tailored to your animal, especially before travel, outdoor activity, or a major change in routine.

Warning signs of heat illness

Watch for unusual or heavy panting, excessive drooling, fast or difficult breathing, weakness, unusual tiredness, vomiting, diarrhoea, stumbling, confusion, collapse, or seizures. Cats may show less obvious changes, such as marked weakness, rapid breathing, or hiding. Do not wait for every sign to appear.

Important: Suspected heatstroke is an emergency. Contact a veterinarian or the nearest emergency veterinary clinic immediately and follow their instructions. Do not delay professional care to see whether your pet improves on their own.

What to do if you are worried

Stop exercise and move your pet away from the heat into a cooler, shaded or air-conditioned place. Call a veterinarian or emergency clinic straight away and explain what happened and what signs you can see. Follow their instructions about safe cooling and transport; recommendations can depend on the animal's condition. If possible, have someone call ahead while you arrange prompt transport.

Do not force water into an animal that is weak, confused, vomiting, or unable to swallow normally. Do not give human medicines. Even if your pet seems to recover, a suspected heat illness still needs veterinary advice because complications may not be obvious at first.

Make the plan fit your local climate

In humid tropical regions, pay close attention to humidity and airflow, not just the thermometer. In dry, sunny regions, provide shade and protect paws from hot ground. During travel, check the forecast at every stop and never assume that a comfortable morning will stay comfortable in a parked vehicle. In cooler countries, an unexpected warm spell can still catch pets and owners off guard.

entry.title: Indoor Cat Enrichment: 8 Easy Ways to Keep Your Cat Happy | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Discover eight practical indoor cat enrichment ideas, from interactive play and food puzzles to climbing spaces, scratching spots and safer daily routines.
entry.content:
← Pawwise Daily home

CAT WELLBEING GUIDE · 8 MIN READ

Indoor cat enrichment: 8 easy ways to make every day more interesting

A happy indoor life is about more than toys. Give your cat safe choices to hunt, climb, scratch, hide, watch the world and spend time with you.

Updated November 19, 2026 · Pawwise Daily Editorial Team

Indoor cats can enjoy safe, comfortable lives, but a predictable room with little to explore may leave some cats under-stimulated. Enrichment means giving a cat appropriate opportunities to use natural behaviours: stalking, chasing, pouncing, searching for food, climbing, scratching, hiding and choosing when to interact.

There is no single perfect setup. A confident young cat may enjoy energetic games, while a shy, older or less mobile cat may prefer quiet hiding places and easy-to-reach resting spots. Start small, watch your cat’s response and keep activities positive.

In this guide
  1. Interactive play
  2. Food puzzles and foraging
  3. Boxes and hiding places
  4. Climbing and window views
  5. Scratching choices
  6. Rotate toys
  7. Multi-cat and age-aware setups
  8. Safety first

1. Make time for short interactive play

Use a wand toy or soft toy that can be moved like prey: let it travel along the floor, disappear briefly behind a cushion, then move away. Give your cat chances to stalk, chase and catch it. Several short sessions may suit some cats better than one long session; let your cat set the pace and stop if they lose interest or seem tired.

Keep hands and feet out of the game. Use a toy between your hands and your cat, and finish by allowing a catch. If your cat enjoys it, offer a small part of their normal daily food allowance afterwards.

2. Turn part of mealtime into a search game

Try placing a small portion of your cat’s usual measured food in a few easy-to-find spots or using a suitable puzzle feeder. Begin with a simple puzzle and show your cat how it works. Make it easier if they become frustrated.

Count puzzle food and treats as part of the daily ration. Check that your cat is actually eating enough, especially if they are elderly, unwell, underweight or on a prescribed diet. Do not suddenly make food difficult to reach.

3. Offer boxes, tunnels and quiet hiding places

A clean cardboard box, a paper bag with handles removed, or a cat tunnel can become a place to investigate, hide or rest. Put one in a calm area and let your cat approach it voluntarily. A familiar blanket can make a new resting spot more inviting.

Every cat should have a safe retreat where they will not be disturbed. Never pull a hiding cat out to make them play or meet visitors.

4. Add safe climbing and window-watching options

Many cats enjoy looking down from a stable perch. A secure cat tree, sturdy shelf or window seat can add useful vertical space. Make sure furniture cannot wobble or tip, and keep the route up and down manageable. For older cats or cats with mobility limits, provide lower steps or ramps rather than expecting big jumps.

A window view can provide changing sights and sounds. Secure windows and screens so your cat cannot fall or escape, and make sure the perch does not overheat in direct sun.

5. Give your cat more than one scratching surface

Scratching is normal cat behaviour. Offer a stable vertical post and, if your cat prefers it, a horizontal cardboard or sisal scratcher. Place options near sleeping areas or places your cat already likes to scratch. Reward interest with praise or a treat; do not punish scratching.

6. Rotate toys instead of leaving everything out

Keep a small selection available and put some toys away for a few days before bringing them back. Try different textures and movements, but avoid toys with loose pieces that could be chewed off. A simple paper ball may delight one cat while another prefers a soft kicker toy.

7. Adjust enrichment for your cat and household

For kittens, choose sturdy, age-appropriate toys and supervise active play. Older cats may still enjoy play, but gentler movement, shorter sessions and easy access to resources can help. If your cat has arthritis, heart or breathing disease, or another medical condition, ask your veterinarian what level of activity is appropriate.

In homes with more than one cat, provide multiple separated resting, feeding, water, litter and scratching locations. Give each cat a chance to play individually if they prefer it. One cat should not be able to block another from reaching food, litter or a safe resting place.

8. Keep enrichment safe

  • Put away wand toys, string, ribbon, thread, elastic bands and anything that could be swallowed after supervised play.
  • Avoid small detachable parts, sharp edges, plastic bags and toys that are damaged or shedding pieces.
  • If you use a laser toy, finish by directing your cat to a physical toy or treat they can catch; do not leave the game unresolved.
  • Keep food puzzles clean and use materials that cannot splinter or break into swallowable pieces.
  • Secure balconies, windows, shelves and heavy furniture. Check that houseplants are cat-safe before bringing them indoors.
When to ask your veterinarian: A sudden drop in play, new hiding, irritability, unusual vocalising, changes in appetite or toileting, or difficulty jumping can have a medical cause. Do not assume boredom is the explanation. Arrange a veterinary check, especially if the change is sudden or persistent.

A simple 10-minute enrichment routine

2 minutesOffer a short wand-toy game and let your cat catch the toy.
2 minutesHide a few pieces of their measured food in easy places.
3 minutesInvite exploration of a box, tunnel or scratching post.
3 minutesLet your cat choose a perch, window view or quiet rest.

This is only a starting point, not a required schedule. Some cats want more activity; others prefer a little at a time. Consistency and choice matter more than expensive equipment.

Frequently asked questions

How much play does an indoor cat need?

There is no exact number that suits every cat. Offer regular opportunities for short interactive sessions and adjust length and intensity to your cat’s age, health and interest.

Do I need to buy expensive enrichment toys?

No. A sturdy cardboard box, safe paper ball, simple hiding game or homemade puzzle made from safe materials can be useful. Supervise homemade items and discard anything damaged.

My cat ignores toys. What should I do?

Try a different movement, texture or time of day. Some cats prefer slow ground-level movement, food searches, watching birds from a secure window or simply having a quiet hiding place. Never force interaction.

Remember: the best enrichment is safe, varied and chosen around the individual cat. For more everyday basics, read our complete cat care guide and our cat-friendly litter box guide.

Trusted further reading

  • AAFP and ISFM Feline Environmental Needs Guidelines
  • VCA Animal Hospitals: Enrichment for Indoor Cats
  • Cats Protection: Cat enrichment advice

This article is general educational information, not veterinary diagnosis or treatment. Every cat is different; consult a licensed veterinarian for individual advice.

entry.title: Dog Separation Anxiety: Signs and Gentle Ways to Help | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Learn common signs of separation anxiety in dogs, how to monitor distress, build alone-time gradually, avoid harmful responses and know when to contact a veterinarian.
entry.content:
🐾 Pawwise Daily

Dog behaviour · Gentle training

Dog separation anxiety: signs and gentle ways to help

If your dog barks, paces, chews or seems distressed when you leave, they may be struggling with being alone. The first step is to understand what is happening—not to punish the behaviour.

Published November 19, 2026 · Pawwise Daily Editorial Team

Some dogs settle comfortably when left at home. Others find separation difficult and may show signs of distress soon after a person leaves. Separation-related behaviour is not spite or a dog trying to get revenge. It is a sign that the dog may be struggling to cope.

Not every bark, accident or chewed object means separation anxiety. Noise outside, incomplete toilet training, boredom, pain and other health or behaviour concerns can look similar. Look for a pattern and, when in doubt, ask a veterinarian to help identify the cause.

In this guide
  1. Signs to look for
  2. Understand what happens when you leave
  3. A gentle starting plan
  4. What not to do
  5. When to seek professional help
  6. Common questions

1. Signs your dog may be distressed when alone

Possible signs include persistent barking, whining or howling; pacing or being unable to settle; panting, trembling or drooling; scratching or chewing near doors and windows; attempts to escape; toileting indoors despite being house-trained; or refusing food that they normally enjoy. Some dogs show distress before the person has even left, when they notice keys, shoes or other departure cues.

These signs matter most when they reliably happen during separation and are not explained by another trigger. A dog that destroys one cushion while people are home may have a different problem from a dog that repeatedly scratches the exit door only after everyone leaves.

2. Find out what happens after you leave

If it is safe and practical, use a camera or an old phone placed securely to record a short period after departure. Watch for when signs begin, what seems to trigger them, whether your dog can eat or rest, and whether they recover. Do not leave a dog in a situation that is already causing severe distress just to collect a recording.

Keep a simple note of the time you leave, how long your dog remains settled, the first sign of stress and any outside events such as delivery noise. This information can help your veterinarian or behaviour professional.

3. Start with very small, comfortable steps

The aim is not to make your dog endure a long absence. It is to practise separations so brief that your dog can remain relaxed, then build gradually at a pace they can handle.

  1. Choose a comfortable resting area. Offer water, familiar bedding and safe activities. A crate is not automatically the answer; if confinement causes panting, frantic escape attempts or more distress, do not force it.
  2. Notice your dog’s calm baseline. Practise short periods of relaxing on a bed while you are still at home. Reward calm behaviour and let your dog choose to rest.
  3. Make departure signals less worrying. If keys or shoes trigger anxiety, sometimes pick them up without leaving. Keep these practice moments easy and stop if your dog becomes worried.
  4. Begin with a tiny separation. Step behind an interior door or briefly out of sight, then return while your dog is still calm. For some dogs this may be only a second or two.
  5. Increase only when your dog stays relaxed. Repeat easy steps and change the duration gradually. If you see stress, make the next practice shorter or easier. There is no universal timetable.
  6. Use food toys only if your dog is comfortable eating. A safe food puzzle can make a mild separation more pleasant for some dogs, but it is not a cure and may not help a dog who is too anxious to eat.
Remember: Progress is measured by relaxed behaviour, not by how many minutes you can stay away. A few calm seconds are a better starting point than a long, frightening absence.

4. Avoid responses that can make things worse

  • Do not punish barking, chewing or toileting after you return. Your dog may become more frightened without understanding what you are upset about.
  • Do not use a “cry it out” approach or deliberately leave your dog to panic.
  • Do not suddenly increase alone time because one practice session went well.
  • Do not assume extra exercise alone will resolve separation anxiety. Exercise and enrichment support wellbeing, but they do not replace an appropriate behaviour plan.
  • Do not give human medication, sedatives or supplements unless your veterinarian has advised it.

5. When to contact a veterinarian

Arrange a veterinary appointment if the behaviour is new, persistent, getting worse or accompanied by changes in appetite, toileting, sleep, movement or general health. Seek help promptly if your dog injures themselves trying to escape, breaks teeth or nails, becomes extremely distressed, or cannot settle even during very short separations.

A veterinarian can check for medical contributors and, when needed, refer you to a qualified veterinary behaviourist or appropriately credentialed behaviour professional. Moderate or severe cases often need an individual plan; medication may sometimes be considered by a veterinarian as part of treatment.

Urgent safety: If your dog has injured themselves, is struggling to breathe, collapses or may have swallowed something toxic, seek urgent veterinary care.

6. Frequently asked questions

Will my dog grow out of separation anxiety?

Do not rely on the problem disappearing by itself. Early support can prevent repeated distress and help identify the right approach.

Should I get another dog to keep mine company?

Not as a first-line fix. Separation distress is often linked to being apart from a particular person, so another pet may not solve it. Consider another animal only if you independently want and can care for one.

Is crate training always helpful?

No. Some dogs enjoy a crate when they have learned to feel safe there; others become more distressed when confined. Watch your dog’s response and discuss alternatives with a professional.

How long does improvement take?

There is no reliable one-size-fits-all timeline. It depends on the dog, the severity of distress, the environment and how consistently the plan can keep practice below the dog’s stress threshold.

This article is general educational information, not a diagnosis or treatment plan. A veterinarian who knows your dog can provide individual guidance.

entry.title: Why Does My Dog Keep Licking Their Paws? Causes & What to Do | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Find out why dogs lick their paws, how to check for irritation or injury, what is safe to do at home, and when persistent licking needs a vet.
entry.content:
🐾 Pawwise Daily

Dog health & behaviour · Practical guide

Why Does My Dog Keep Licking Their Paws?

A little paw licking can be normal grooming. Repeated licking, chewing, or focusing on one foot can be a sign of itchiness, irritation, injury, or pain. The pattern—and what the paw looks like—can help you decide what to do next.

Quick answer: Dogs may lick their paws to clean them, but frequent or intense licking can be linked to allergies, irritation, a small injury, parasites, infection, pain, or stress. Check the paw gently. If licking continues, causes skin damage, or comes with limping, swelling, discharge, or a strong smell, contact your veterinarian.
Share this guide: Facebook · WhatsApp · LinkedIn
In this guide
  • When paw licking is normal
  • Common reasons dogs lick their paws
  • How to check your dog's paw safely
  • When to contact a veterinarian
  • What not to do

When paw licking is normal

Dogs use their mouths to explore and groom. A brief lick after a walk, after eating, or when cleaning away a little dirt may be ordinary. It is more concerning when your dog returns to the same paw again and again, chews intensely, cannot be distracted, wakes up to lick, or creates red, damp, sore, or hairless skin.

Common reasons dogs lick their paws

1. Allergies or skin irritation

Environmental allergens, contact irritants, and some food-related sensitivities can make paws itchy. You may also notice licking on several feet, scratching elsewhere, or recurring ear and skin problems. A veterinarian can help work out the cause; do not start an elimination diet or medication without professional guidance.

2. A small injury or something stuck

A thorn, grass seed, splinter, tiny cut, insect sting, cracked pad, or damaged nail can make one paw suddenly uncomfortable. Licking that starts abruptly and focuses on one foot deserves a careful look.

3. Infection or inflammation

Repeated moisture and irritation can damage the skin. Redness, swelling, discharge, a strong or unusual smell, sores, or brown saliva staining may indicate a problem that needs veterinary assessment. Do not assume you can identify a yeast or bacterial infection by appearance alone.

4. Pain in the paw or leg

Dogs sometimes lick an area that hurts. Watch for limping, stiffness, reluctance to jump or use stairs, holding a paw up, or reacting when the leg or foot is touched. Pain may not be obvious from the skin surface.

5. Stress, boredom, or a repetitive habit

Some dogs lick to self-soothe, particularly during stressful periods or when they are under-stimulated. However, medical causes such as itchiness and pain should be considered first. Behavioural and physical factors can also occur together.

How to check your dog's paw safely

  1. Choose a calm moment and let your dog settle. Stop if handling causes pain or distress.
  2. Look at the top and underside of the paw, between the toes, around the pads, and around each nail.
  3. Check for redness, swelling, cuts, broken nails, damp skin, discharge, odour, or visible debris.
  4. If the paw is simply dirty and there is no open wound, gently rinse with clean lukewarm water and dry carefully, including between the toes.
  5. Note when the licking began, whether it affects one paw or several, and any changes in walking, appetite, or energy.
Do not dig into the skin. If something is embedded, difficult to remove, or painful, leave it in place and contact a veterinary clinic.

When to contact a veterinarian

Arrange a veterinary appointment if licking is persistent or repeatedly returns, or if you notice redness, swelling, hair loss, sores, a bad smell, discharge, a damaged nail, or limping. Sudden severe pain, inability to put weight on the leg, heavy bleeding, a deep wound, rapidly increasing swelling, or suspected chemical exposure needs urgent veterinary advice.

If your dog seems otherwise well but keeps licking, do not wait until the skin is raw. Early assessment can help identify the underlying cause and prevent further irritation.

What not to do

  • Do not apply human creams, essential oils, disinfectants, or pain-relief products unless your veterinarian specifically recommends them.
  • Do not give human painkillers or leftover pet medication.
  • Do not tightly wrap the paw or force your dog to wear a boot if it causes distress.
  • Do not punish or scold licking. It is a sign to investigate, not misbehaviour.

Helpful everyday habits

After walks, check paws for mud, burrs, grit, and small cuts. During seasons when grass or pollen bothers your dog, ask your veterinarian whether a gentle paw rinse after outdoor time is suitable. Keep nails at a comfortable length and provide regular exercise, sniffing, play, and rest. These habits support comfort but do not replace diagnosis when licking persists.

entry.title: Why Do Cats Scratch Furniture? Kind Ways to Redirect the Habit | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Learn why cats scratch sofas and chairs, how to protect furniture, choose scratching posts, and guide your cat toward better scratching spots without punishment.
entry.content:
🐾 Pawwise Daily

Cat behaviour · Practical home guide

Why Do Cats Scratch Furniture?

A scratched sofa is frustrating, but scratching is a normal cat behaviour—not spite or revenge. Cats scratch to maintain their claws, stretch, leave scent and visual marks, and express excitement. The goal is not to stop scratching altogether. It is to make the right places more appealing.

The simple plan: Put a sturdy scratching post right beside the furniture your cat targets, choose a texture and orientation your cat likes, reward use, and temporarily protect the furniture. Keep the approved scratching spot available every day.
Share this guide: Facebook · WhatsApp · LinkedIn
In this guide
  • Why cats scratch
  • Choose a scratching post
  • Redirect furniture scratching
  • What to avoid
  • When to ask for help

Why cats scratch

Scratching is part of normal feline behaviour. It helps loosen and remove the outer sheath of the claws, gives the body a satisfying stretch, and leaves scent and visible marks. Cats may scratch after waking, during play, when excited, or near places where people and pets move through the home. A favourite sofa corner may simply have the right texture, height, location, or stability.

Choose a scratching post your cat will actually use

  • Make it stable. A post that wobbles or tips can make a cat avoid it. Choose a heavy base or secure it safely.
  • Match the direction. If your cat stretches up a sofa arm, try a tall vertical post. If they scratch rugs, offer a horizontal or angled scratcher.
  • Try different textures. Sisal, corrugated cardboard, and sturdy carpet-like materials feel different. Offer a choice and observe what your cat prefers.
  • Make it long enough. A vertical post should allow a comfortable full-body stretch.
  • Put it in the right place. Start beside the target furniture, near a sleeping spot, or in a well-used room—not hidden away in a rarely visited corner.

How to redirect scratching away from furniture

  1. Place the new scratcher directly beside the area your cat scratches. If necessary, add another scratcher at a second favourite location.
  2. Make the furniture less rewarding temporarily with a purpose-made, pet-safe furniture protector. Check it often and follow the product instructions.
  3. When your cat uses the scratcher, offer calm praise, play, or a small treat if appropriate. You can use a toy to invite exploration, but never force the paws onto the post.
  4. Keep the scratcher clean and stable. Replace worn cardboard or damaged posts before they become unattractive or unsafe.
  5. Once the scratcher is used reliably, move it gradually if you need it in a different location—just a little at a time.
Helpful tip: Cats often scratch after waking. Placing a scratcher near a favourite sleeping place can make the appropriate choice convenient at exactly the right moment.

What not to do

  • Do not yell, spray water, hit, or frighten your cat. Punishment can create fear and does not teach which surface to use.
  • Do not declaw as a furniture solution. Declawing is an amputation procedure, not a nail trim; discuss humane claw-care and behaviour options with a veterinarian.
  • Do not use sticky materials, scents, or deterrent products unless they are specifically labelled safe for cats and used as directed.
  • Do not remove every scratching option. Scratching is a normal need; provide suitable alternatives.

When to ask for help

If scratching behaviour changes suddenly, your cat seems distressed, damages their claws, avoids using a paw, or has skin or nail problems, arrange a veterinary check. If your cat scratches people or other pets, or the behaviour is causing serious household stress, a veterinarian or qualified feline behaviour professional can help you build a safe plan.

Quick home checklist

  • At least one stable scratcher near the furniture being targeted.
  • More than one texture or orientation if you are unsure what your cat prefers.
  • Daily play and predictable opportunities to climb, explore, and rest.
  • Positive rewards for using approved scratching surfaces.
  • Regular checks of claws, paws, and scratcher condition.

Related Pawwise Daily guides

  • Cat care basics
  • Indoor enrichment ideas for cats
  • How to set up a cat-friendly litter box
  • Why dogs lick their paws

Choosing a suitable scratching surface

Once you understand why your cat scratches, offer a surface that matches their habits. Read our cat scratching post buying guide for help comparing vertical posts, horizontal boards, materials, stability and placement.

entry.title: How to Choose a Cat Scratching Post: A Practical Buying Guide | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Choose a cat scratching post that your cat will actually use. Compare vertical, horizontal and angled designs, materials, height, stability and placement.
entry.content:
🐾 Pawwise Daily

CAT CARE · BUYING GUIDE

How to Choose a Cat Scratching Post

The right scratching surface can protect your furniture and give your cat a healthy place to stretch, scratch and mark their territory. Here is what to look for before you buy.

Choose a scratching area that fits your cat's natural habits and your home's layout.

Quick answer: Start with a sturdy post that allows a full-body stretch, or a horizontal cardboard scratcher if your cat prefers floor-level surfaces. Stability and your cat's preference matter more than appearance.
In this guide
  1. Why the right scratcher matters
  2. Choose the right shape
  3. Compare common materials
  4. Check height and stability
  5. Put it in the right place
  6. Buying mistakes to avoid
  7. Frequently asked questions

Why the right scratcher matters

Scratching is normal cat behaviour. Cats use it to maintain their claws, stretch their bodies and leave scent and visual marks. A scratching post is not simply a toy: it gives your cat an appropriate surface for an instinctive activity.

If your cat scratches a sofa, the goal is not to punish the behaviour. It is to make an acceptable scratching surface more appealing and easier to use. For practical ways to redirect the habit, read our guide to why cats scratch furniture.

1. Choose the right shape for your cat

Vertical posts

A vertical post is a good starting point for cats that stand up and stretch when scratching. Look for enough height for a long stretch, plus a broad, secure base. A narrow post that rocks every time your cat uses it may be ignored.

Horizontal scratchers

Flat cardboard or sisal boards suit cats that scratch rugs, mats or other floor-level surfaces. They can also fit easily in smaller rooms. Check that the board does not slide around during use.

Angled or ramp-style scratchers

An angled surface offers a middle option for cats that like to scratch at a slope. It may be useful when your cat ignores both a straight post and a flat board.

Multi-level cat trees

A cat tree can combine scratching, climbing and resting. Choose one with a stable footprint and platforms appropriate for your cat's size and mobility. More features are not automatically better if the structure wobbles.

2. Compare common scratching materials

MaterialOften suitsWhat to check
Sisal rope or fabricCats that enjoy a firm, textured vertical surfaceSecure attachment, no loose strands, and a surface tall enough to use comfortably.
Corrugated cardboardCats that like horizontal scratching and a softer feelSturdy construction, low movement, and easy replacement when worn.
CarpetSome cats that already choose carpet-like texturesA distinct texture from household carpet can help avoid confusing the target.
Wood or other firm surfacesCats with a clear preference for firm surfacesSmooth, safe edges and a stable design without splinters.

There is no universal winner. If possible, notice what your cat already scratches: vertical upholstery, carpet, cardboard packaging or a rough mat. Use that clue to choose the first surface to try.

3. Check height, base and build quality

  • Enough height: A vertical post should let your cat extend its body comfortably.
  • A wide, heavy base: The post should stay upright when your cat leans into it.
  • Secure materials: Avoid loose cords, exposed staples, sharp edges and pieces that can be chewed off and swallowed.
  • Appropriate size: A large or energetic cat may need a sturdier, larger scratcher than a small kitten.
  • Easy upkeep: Replace damaged cardboard and repair or replace worn surfaces before they become unsafe.
Safety note: Stop using a scratcher if it becomes unstable, has sharp broken parts, or sheds pieces that your cat may swallow. For kittens, older cats or cats with mobility concerns, choose a design that is easy to approach and use.

4. Put the scratcher where your cat wants to use it

Even a well-made post can be ignored if it is hidden in an unused corner. Place a new scratcher near the sofa, chair or doorway your cat already targets. Many cats also like a scratching surface near a favourite sleeping area because stretching and scratching often happen after waking.

If your cat uses the new surface, reward the choice with calm praise, play or a small treat if appropriate. You can make the old target less appealing temporarily while keeping the new scratcher close by. Avoid shouting, spraying water or physically forcing your cat's paws onto the post.

5. Buying mistakes to avoid

  • Choosing a post only because it matches the room, without checking whether it is stable.
  • Buying a short vertical post that does not allow a full stretch.
  • Assuming every cat likes sisal; some prefer cardboard or another texture.
  • Putting the scratcher far away from the place where scratching already happens.
  • Buying a complex cat tree when a simple, sturdy board would better match your cat's habits.

Frequently asked questions

How tall should a cat scratching post be?

Choose a post that lets your cat stretch close to full length without making it wobble. Larger cats usually need a taller and sturdier design.

Is sisal or cardboard better?

Neither is best for every cat. Sisal suits many cats that prefer a firm vertical surface; corrugated cardboard often appeals to cats that scratch horizontally. Your cat's preference is the best guide.

Where should I put a scratching post?

Start near the furniture or doorway your cat already scratches. You can add another near a favourite sleeping spot if your home has room.

How many scratchers does a cat need?

Offer more than one suitable scratching location when possible, especially in a multi-room home or a home with several cats. Put them in places your cat naturally spends time.

Final checklist before you buy

Choose a shape that matches your cat's habits, a texture your cat may enjoy, a stable base, a safe finish and a location near an existing scratching spot. If your first choice is ignored, try a different orientation or material rather than assuming your cat cannot learn to use a scratcher.

This guide is general educational information, not veterinary advice. If scratching behaviour changes suddenly or comes with signs of pain, ask a veterinarian.

entry.title: How to Choose a Dog Harness: Fit, Style and Safety Guide | Pawwise Daily
entry.summary: Learn how to choose a comfortable dog harness. Compare Y-front, step-in and vest styles, measure your dog, check fit and avoid common buying mistakes.
entry.content:
🐾 Pawwise Daily

DOG CARE · BUYING GUIDE

How to Choose a Dog Harness

A comfortable harness should fit your dog’s body, allow natural movement and stay secure on walks. Use this guide to compare styles, measure carefully and check the fit before every outing.

A well-fitted harness should stay secure without rubbing or limiting your dog’s movement. Photo: Jonathan Cooper / Pexels.

Quick answer: Measure your dog rather than guessing by breed or weight. Choose a harness that sits securely around the chest, does not press into the throat or armpits, and lets your dog walk naturally. Always check the manufacturer’s size chart.
In this guide
  1. Compare common harness styles
  2. Measure your dog correctly
  3. Check comfort and fit
  4. Understand leash attachment points
  5. Safety and care checks
  6. Buying mistakes to avoid
  7. Frequently asked questions

1. Compare common dog harness styles

Y-front or chest-shaped harnesses

These are designed with straps that form a shape around the front of the chest. Look for a design that leaves the shoulder area free to move and does not press across the throat. The label alone does not guarantee a good fit: check how the specific harness sits on your dog.

Step-in harnesses

Your dog places its front paws through openings before the harness is fastened around the back. This can be convenient for dogs that dislike having equipment slipped over their head. Check that the straps stay in position and that your dog cannot back out of it.

Vest or padded harnesses

These spread contact across a broader area and may suit some dogs, but thick padding can become warm or rub if the shape is wrong. Check the fit around the chest and behind the front legs, especially in warm weather.

Escape-resistant designs

Some harnesses include an additional strap around the waist or extra adjustment points. They may be worth considering for dogs that can reverse out of ordinary harnesses. No design should be treated as escape-proof; check every buckle and fit before walking.

2. Measure your dog before choosing a size

  1. Use a flexible measuring tape and keep your dog standing naturally.
  2. Measure the chest girth around the widest part of the rib cage, usually just behind the front legs.
  3. Measure the neck only if the manufacturer's chart requests it, and follow its exact measuring position.
  4. Compare the measurements with that brand's size chart. Sizes are not consistent between manufacturers.
  5. If your dog falls between sizes, follow the brand's fitting guidance or contact the maker before ordering.

Weight and breed can be useful background information, but they cannot replace measurements. Two dogs of the same breed can have very different chest shapes, coat thickness and proportions.

3. Check comfort and fit after putting it on

  • Secure, not restrictive: The harness should not squeeze the rib cage or make breathing uncomfortable.
  • Keep the throat clear: Straps should not ride up and press against the neck when the leash becomes taut.
  • Watch the armpits: Straps that sit too close to the front legs can rub during walking.
  • Allow natural movement: Watch your dog walk, turn and sit. Look for shortened steps, awkward shoulder movement or reluctance.
  • Check for rubbing: After a short walk, inspect the skin and coat under the straps for redness, hair loss or damp, irritated areas.
  • Check security: The harness should not twist, slide over the head or allow your dog to back out.
Important: Do not rely on a universal “two-finger rule” as the only fit test. Harness construction differs. Follow the manufacturer's fitting instructions and make sure the harness is secure without restricting breathing or movement.

4. Understand front and back leash attachments

A back attachment is commonly used for everyday walking when a dog is comfortable on leash. A front attachment may help some handlers guide a dog that pulls by changing the direction of the leash, but it is not a substitute for training and can affect movement if used incorrectly.

Some harnesses offer both attachment points. Choose based on your dog's behaviour, body shape and your ability to handle the leash safely. If your dog lunges, is very strong, or has neck, back or mobility problems, ask a veterinarian or qualified force-free trainer for individual advice.

5. Safety and care checks

  • Inspect stitching, buckles, adjustment sliders and leash rings regularly.
  • Replace a harness with cracked hardware, frayed straps or damaged fasteners.
  • Choose reflective details or add visibility accessories for walks in low light.
  • Keep identification details current; a harness is not a substitute for a collar tag or microchip where appropriate.
  • Remove the harness when it is not needed unless its maker or your veterinarian advises otherwise. Check for trapped moisture and rubbing.
  • Introduce a new harness gradually with treats and calm praise. Never force a frightened dog into it.

6. Buying mistakes to avoid

  • Choosing by breed name or weight without measuring chest girth.
  • Assuming a padded or expensive harness must be more comfortable.
  • Ignoring the space behind the front legs, where rubbing can occur.
  • Buying a harness that is easy to put on but easy for the dog to escape from.
  • Using a front-clip attachment as the only solution to pulling.
  • Leaving a wet or dirty harness on without checking the skin underneath.

Frequently asked questions

How do I measure my dog for a harness?

Use a soft measuring tape and follow the brand's chart. Most harnesses use chest girth around the widest part of the rib cage, just behind the front legs. Some also require a neck measurement.

Should a dog harness be tight or loose?

It should be secure without squeezing, rubbing or restricting movement. Follow the maker's instructions and check your dog's skin and coat after use.

Is a front-clip harness better for pulling?

A front attachment may help some handlers redirect a dog, but it does not teach loose-leash walking on its own. Reward-based training and safe handling are still important.

Can a dog wear a harness all day?

Many harnesses are intended for walks rather than continuous wear. Remove it when it is not needed unless the maker or your veterinarian advises otherwise, and check for rubbing or trapped moisture.

Final checklist before you buy

Measure your dog, compare the maker's chart, inspect the harness shape around the chest and shoulders, check the adjustment range and hardware, and test the fit with a short supervised walk. If your dog moves awkwardly, rubs, freezes or tries to escape, stop and reassess the design or fit.

This guide is general educational information, not veterinary or training advice. Ask a veterinarian or qualified humane trainer about your dog's individual needs.
